item.description:
Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says

Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.

“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.

“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”

The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.

The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.

Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an “epidemiological alert” across the territory, warning that a “shocking” increase in meningitis infections puts hundreds of thousands of lives at risk, particularly children.

The ministry urged the World Health Organization and Unicef to launch an emergency response.

Dr Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for public health, reported 272 cases in October. He described the figure as more than eight times the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.

Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the August-to-October surge.

The ministry described the outbreak as an “inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain”.

“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilization materials and fuel,” it said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
item.description:
How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Sun, 11/22/2026 - 19:03
Experts warn that spyware used by Israel on Palestinians is being exported to US and European governments for state repression at home
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar (L) addresses a press conference after a meeting at the EU headquarters on the sidelines of the EU's foreign affairs council in Brussels, 24 February 2025 (John Thys/AFP)
Off

This week, the Geneva Convention held its Seventh Review Conference on the development of technological warfare and its humanitarian implications.

The review takes place every five years and aims to negotiate legally binding international agreements on restricting autonomous weapon systems, amid growing concerns over their use against civilians. However, powerful militarised countries like the US and Russia generally block progress.

Since the last review, the use of AI-powered weapons has accelerated exponentially, with much of the cutting-edge technology being used by Israelis against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by Israel.

Despite this, Palestine was barely mentioned during the UN meeting.

Last week, the Palestinian digital rights organisation 7amleh organised a conference in Brussels, attended by Middle East Eye, bringing together policymakers, journalists, politicians and researchers to assess the use of autonomous weapons in the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Nadim Nashif, 7amleh’s executive director, told the conference that Palestine is treated as a “laboratory” for AI, with technologies tested on Palestinians before being sold around the world and marketed as “battlefield-tested”.

Palestinians are among the most surveilled people on earth. Even before the genocide, he said, they were subjected to Israeli facial recognition and phone hacking, living in a “panopticon” of round-the-clock “mass surveillance”.

However, “what happened in Palestine does not stay in Palestine”, Nashif added, warning of the dangers of “having the power in the hands of a few people…controlling the future of humanity” without regulation or accountability.

Imperial boomerang

“Gaza is a trial for these technologies,” Member of European Parliament (MEP) Benedetta Scuderi told the conference.

Scuderi argued that European defence agreements with Israel undermine international regulations.

“When technology comes in… humanity goes away,” she said, warning that “if we lose humanity then we are done”. 

Scuderi referenced the European parliament’s recent screening of Israeli film NAZA, a documentary compiling interviews with Israeli army officials on the uses of these technologies in Gaza.

One soldier described feeling like he was in a “video game” when using technology such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy to locate and target Palestinians.

European countries remain complicit through their involvement in production, research and arms sales to Israel, as exemptions allow European weapons to be exported despite their use in facilitating genocide, according to a 2025 UN report.

Scuderi called for human rights reviews of European budgets, acknowledging that even getting such measures “on paper” is difficult, with those in power viewing them as “an extra burden”.

Without regulation, she warned, technologies developed by western governments and used by Israel against Palestinians will inevitably be deployed domestically against journalists and activists, including in her home country of Italy. This phenomenon is known as the imperial boomerang.

Meanwhile, EU taxpayers continue to fund Israeli projects. In 2025, Israeli companies, universities and research institutes received €106m from the EU’s Horizon Europe fund.

Israel's arms industry thrives on genocide and the world keeps buying
Read More »

At the conference, Harry Davies, a Guardian journalist and producer of NAZA, discussed a report he co-wrote with the documentary’s creator, Yuval Abraham, on Israel’s use of Microsoft cloud servers to store “a million calls an hour” made by Palestinians in the occupied territories.

In 2021, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella met the head of Israel’s military surveillance agency, Unit 8200, to arrange for vast amounts of data to be stored on Microsoft’s servers.

Following the investigation, Microsoft confirmed the findings and terminated its deal with the Israeli army, demonstrating the impact of journalism and public scrutiny.

While NAZA presents no new claims or information that Palestinians have not reported on for years, Davies said, it is “less about the actual technology than the people behind them, and the military systems” that enable the mass automated killing in Gaza.

In response, the Israeli army presented the technologies as mere tools, insisting decisions remain with military personnel.

The film shows “how meaningful that human involvement is”, Davies said, warning that relying on machine-generated statistical calculations can reinforce preconceived biases when operated in an atmosphere “of hatred and revenge”.

Failure of EU regulation

At the 7amleh conference, researchers from European Digital Rights revealed that 15 out of 27 European countries were discovered to have breached EU spyware regulations, with victims coming from civil society groups, journalists and political opponents. 

In Spain, at least 65 individuals - including members of the European Parliament, Catalan presidents, legislators, jurists and members of civil society organisations - were allegedly targeted by the government using Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group. The government initially denied the allegations but later acknowledged spying on 18 individuals, citing national security concerns.

'Gaza is a trial for these technologies'

- Benedetta Scuderi, Member of European Parliament 

In Poland, Pegasus spyware was used to target almost 600 people between 2017 and 2022 under the former Law and Justice government, “too many” of whom were targeted for being “inconvenient”, according to the current security services minister.

Following the scandal, the European Parliament launched the Pega committee in 2022 to investigate Pegasus and other spyware against civil society. However, its recommendations were never implemented. 

Tech watchdog Citizen Lab found that a former MEP serving on the committee was hacked with Pegasus spyware at least three times during the investigation.

The European case in which an executive faced consequences was Greece’s 2022 spying scandal, known as “Predatorgate”, which came to light when opposition leader Nikos Androulakis discovered that his phone had been targeted with illegal spyware.

In February, a Greek court sentenced four people, including two Israelis, to prison, although an appeal remains pending.

One of the biggest obstacles to prosecution is gathering evidence, as defence and intelligence contracts are often highly classified. Another is the ability of transnational corporations to change jurisdictions to evade regulation.

Cases subsequently stall, with the EU failing to pursue them. 

‘Free Europe’

In 2017, Project Maven was launched by the US to accelerate AI military intelligence, using Google as a key contractor. But following public pressure, including from its own employees, Google terminated the contract and formulated ethical policies. 

The contract was subsequently taken over by Palantir, which operated Maven during the US abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and the US bombing campaign against Iran. The latter included the “double-tap” strike on a girls’ school in Minab, which killed more than 170 people.

Palantir also holds a contract with the Israeli army, as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is deeply embedded in UK public services, including the National Health Service (NHS).

In 2020, US President Donald Trump pardoned the CEO of Israeli company Cellebrite for assisting cybercrimes, allowing the company to subsequently secure ICE contracts worth up to $96m.

Serbian police and intelligence forces used Cellebrite technology to extract data from phones belonging to journalists and activists.

In Russia and Kenya, the software was also used to target political opponents of the government.

Paragon Solutions, another Israeli company that supplies phone-hacking and listening devices, saw its $2m contract with ICE revived by Trump after former US President Joe Biden had paused it.

Paragon spyware was used to target European journalists and was investigated by Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee in 2025. The company, however, remains embedded in European markets, amid weak oversight and a reluctance to legislate and enforce regulations.

Pegasus Project: Why I was targeted by Israeli spyware

Technologies battle-tested in Gaza are increasingly used for state repression of migrants, left-wing journalists and politicians, and the Palestine solidarity movement. 

EU leaders are at a “crossroads”, MEP Cecilia Strada told the conference, arguing that they can no longer feign ignorance about their role in facilitating crimes against humanity in Gaza or the use of European technologies to profit from mass slaughter.

The European Commission will review the EU-Israel trade agreement after a petition calling for its full suspension surpassed 1.1 million signatures from EU citizens this week.

In 2025, the European Commission proposed a partial suspension of the agreement, but member states failed to adopt the measure and are unlikely to do so now.

“The relationship with Israeli companies are not the fruit of political ties… they are the infested roots of those ties,” Strada said.

She pointed to Palantir’s lucrative UK contracts, describing them as not only “a threat to our democracies and fundamental rights, but also a fraud”, diverting public money away from public services and into private profit.

After visiting Palestine, Strada said she had witnessed the realities of systematic surveillance and brutality, and began to see parallels in the use of the same technologies in Europe.

“Our role is not to free Palestine, but to free Europe,” she said, so it will be “not us which saved Palestinians, but Palestinians that saved us… from a dark future”.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Egypt's terror list targeting European Muslims echoes Israel and the UAE
item.description:
Egypt's terror list targeting European Muslims echoes Israel and the UAE

Submitted by Farid Hafez on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 17:26
Cairo has designated 35 Muslim associations across Europe as terrorists, months after an Israeli ministry report singled out many of the same names
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi (left) speaks with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden (right) and European Council President Antonio Costa at a dinner in Brussels after the EU-Egypt summit on 22 October 2025 (Simon Wohlfahrt/Pool/AFP)
Off

In September, Egyptian police arrested all six journalists at Matsadaash, a news platform dedicated to fact-checking and investigative reporting. They were accused of spreading misinformation on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, a charge the outlet denies.

The authorities then turned on Mada Masr, one of Egypt's best-known independent news sites. In October, a court ordered the site closed. The following month, its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, faced a retrial on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The same charges brought her a one-year prison sentence in absentia in 2024.

Shaher Ayyad, an editorial board member at the news site al-Manassa, told Reuters: "Independent outlets are often portrayed as lawbreakers or enemies of the state."

Both cases are part of the repression that Amnesty International detailed in its 2025 report, which found that authorities "continued to criminalize dissenting forms of expression and peaceful assembly, targeting journalists, protesters, opposition politicians and others who criticized the government's human rights record or called for political change".

Egypt's record of abuse at home has long been documented. A decade after the former military chief took power, the US State Department's 2024 human rights report called the situation dire.

The department cited credible reports of "torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment; arbitrary arrest and detention", "instances of transnational repression against individuals in another country" and "serious restrictions on freedom of expression and media freedom, including unjustified arrests or prosecutions of journalists and censorship".

The list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions

On 10 November, Egypt went a step further and published a list of 35 associations and 36 individuals that the Cairo Criminal Court has designated as "terrorists".

Strikingly, the list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions, the national, cultural, educational and religious bodies that serve Muslim communities across 27 countries.

At its centre is the Council of European Muslims, formerly the Federation of Islamic Organisations in Europe, an umbrella body founded in 1989 whose members help Muslims practise their faith, preserve their identity and integrate into their societies.

The designations are valid for five years, subject to appeal, extension and removal. They were published just days after Egyptian authorities placed the Muslim Brotherhood permanently on the country's terrorism list, replacing a series of time-limited designations.

For those named, the practical consequences could include restrictions on travel and banking, and a real threat to their personal security.

A European echo

Egypt's latest move has raised fears that it is exporting its crackdown on political dissent and extending its hunt for the Muslim Brotherhood, the movement that won the country's election in 2012 before being ousted the following year by the then defence minister, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

Anas Altikriti, the British-Iraqi founder of the Cordoba Foundation and one of the 36 individuals named, said Arab governments regard the political influence of Muslim communities in the West as a threat. "What you actually do is to shut down Muslim civil society in the West," he told The New Arab.

The Brotherhood bogeyman: How Europe and the US criminalise Muslim civic life
Read More »

In 2014, three years after the Arab Spring uprisings, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others, also designated the Brotherhood a "terrorist organisation".

The list was also published a month after the European Parliament's largest group, the European People's Party, pushed through a non-binding resolution "on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network".

The resolution had support from fellow conservatives, the far right and liberals, and opposition from the social democrats, the Greens and the left.

It explicitly named the Council of European Muslims, along with other Muslim and anti-racist organisations, and called for groups associated with the council to be denied access to EU institutions and removed from the EU's transparency register.

Amnesty International and more than 100 other civil society groups wrote to European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in protest, but the letter has gone unanswered.

Given that those targeted are based in Europe, there is reason to suspect a concerted effort by political forces seeking to criminalise Muslim and anti-racist civic life. The picture, however, is bigger than that.

The global picture

It is a mistake to treat Cairo's terror list as a purely domestic decision, or even a Euro-Arab one. Egypt is better understood as part of a wider geopolitical strategy, the culmination of developments well beyond its borders.

First, Egypt has long wanted the Muslim Brotherhood on western terrorist lists, and some argue Sisi is acting largely on behalf of one of Egypt's main financiers, the UAE.

Second, it is no coincidence that those efforts gained ground under the second Trump administration. In November 2025, the president set in motion the designation of Brotherhood chapters, including Egypt's, as terrorist organisations by executive order rather than legislation.

That gave the Egyptian president the symbolic backing to keep telling a story that looks domestic at first glance.

The UAE, for its part, listed 15 civil society groups in the US and Europe as terrorist organisations in 2014, alongside armed groups such as al-Qaeda, Boko Haram and the Islamic State group.

They included the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights group in the US, and the forerunner of the Council of European Muslims, along with the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium that Cairo has now designated.

Muslim Brotherhood allegations are not a new invention, and they played a major role in November's US midterms, where they were levelled at Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.

In January 2025, the UAE added eight companies registered in the UK and owned by Emirati dissidents and their relatives.

The Israel connection

In February 2026, nine months before Egypt published its list, the Netanyahu government's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism released a report titled "The Muslim Brotherhood Across Europe".

The ministry makes no secret of its purpose. Its report says the ministry "systematically documents activities by those engaged in delegitimization" of Israel, and lists "cooperation with pro-Palestinian organizations" and the promotion of boycotts, sanctions and divestment among its areas of focus.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence

Its research department identified nine "key organizations in Europe".

Three of them appear among the eight Europe-wide associations on the Egyptian court's list: the Council of European Muslims, the European Council for Fatwa and Research, and the European Institute of Human Sciences. The Council of European Muslims is the first organisation named in both documents.

The Israeli ministry's report presents the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium as part of the Brotherhood's European network, and all four are now on Egypt's list. Nearly a third of the 36 individuals the Egyptian court named also appear in the report, including four men it identifies as presidents of the council.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence. It suggests Cairo is working from a script written elsewhere, further reducing the country that once led the Arab world to the role of a vessel for wealthy backers aligned with Israel.
